Beállítom „Újra megjelent az afrikai sertéspestis egy hazai házisertés-állományban” – írta a Facebookon Bóna Szabolcs agrárminiszter. A Nébih augusztus 9-én egy Somogy megyei sertéstelepen, Lakócsán mutatta ki a vírust egy 1850 állatból álló állományban. „A szükséges intézkedéseket azonnal elrendeltük. Az érintett állomány felszámolása folyamatban van, és megkezdődött a járványügyi nyomozás is, hogy a szakemberek feltárják a fertőzés lehetséges forrását és az esetleges terjedés kockázatát” – tájékoztatott Bóna. A telep körül védő- és megfigyelési körzeteket jelöltek ki, ezekben járványügyi korlátozások léptek életbe, amik Somogy és Baranya megye több települését is érintik. A miniszter és a Nébih közleménye is figyelmeztetett: az afrikai sertéspestis emberre nem veszélyes, de a sertésállományokra komoly veszélyt jelent, és jelentős gazdasági károkat okozhat. A hatóság felhívta a sertéstartókat, hogy tartsák zártan az állományaikat, akadályozzák meg, hogy a sertéseik – akár csak közvetve is – vaddisznókkal érintkezzenek, ügyeljenek a telepek be- és kilépési szabályaira, és szokatlan megbetegedés vagy állathalálozás esetén értesítsék a hatóságokat. A sertéspestissel kapcsolatos legfrissebb információkat a Nébih tematikus oldalán lehet követni. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Illustrations by Diana Ejaita Enslaving nation Slavery The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans Written by Morgan Ofori and David Conn ; Animation by Alexander Purcell; Photography by Wayne Crichlow Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.03 EDT Share Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls. The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards. The Register of British Slave Traders , a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries. It reveals how wealthy individuals , often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country. Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register had established connections with roughly 900 organisations. “Most of those organisations sought to improve the lives of ordinary Britons,” he added. The register reveals at least 50 people with deep financial ties to St Barts who are directly linked to this history. Among the names etched on to the boards in the Great Hall is Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys, a London merchant who left an unspecified sum to the hospital in his will. In 1694, the Jeffreys-funded ship Hannibal, commanded by Capt Thomas Phillips, docked in Barbados. This concluded a harrowing journey in which only 372 of the 700 enslaved African people bought at Whydah (Ouidah in modern-day Benin) survived the Atlantic crossing. View image in fullscreen The grand Hogarth Stair, which leads to the Great Hall, adorned with paintings depicting healing. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Ornate boards adorn the walls of the Great Hall in St Barts, where governors recorded their philanthropic donations, many while investing in the companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The church of St Bartholomew the Less, in the grounds of St Barts hospital. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A portrait of King Henry VIII in the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, surrounded by the boards commemorating the hospital’s benefactors. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian Phillips’s journal, one of the few surviving records of the voyage, details the horrors onboard, where captives were subjected to branding and calculated psychological cruelty. “Then we marked the slaves we had bought in the breast or shoulder, with a hot iron, having the letter of the ship’s name on it,” he wrote. The Africans on his ship, he recorded, held “a more dreadful apprehension of Barbadoes than we have of hell”. Phillips recalled using African overseers, who were enslaved themselves, to keep order, whipping any plotters of mutiny. There were grave consequences of the squalid conditions on the ship; many who died on the Hannibal were killed by smallpox, dysentery, starvation and suicide. Some were thrown overboard when dead or dying to prevent the spread of disease and to protect profits. The voyage’s mortality rate was close to 50%, cementing its place as one of the deadliest crossings in the history of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. View image in fullscreen A diagram of a ship showing the cramped conditions in which enslaved Africans were trafficked. Composite: Guardian The 1694 Hannibal crossing was one of 13 to which Jeffreys was financially linked. The London merchant was a director of the Royal African Company from 1684-86, and from 1692-98. His latter term coincided with the end of the company’s royal monopoly on trading enslaved Africans, from which he profited handsomely. He also inherited a fortune from his tobacco-trading uncle, John Jeffreys, in 1688. During Jeffrey Jeffreys’ time with the RAC, the organisation made 170 crossings. Others commemorated at St Barts have links to the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Edward Colston, whose statue was toppled by Black Lives Matter protesters in Bristol in June 2020, appears in the register. William Prichard, once president of St Barts and a leading City merchant, bought £600 of RAC stock in January 1678. Sir Robert Geffrye, who left money to the hospital and other philanthropic causes in his will, was a substantial investor in the trafficking of enslaved Africans, selling £1,600 (the equivalent of £350,000 today) of RAC stock on 5 January 1692 alone. Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, has called for the removal of Geffrye’s statue at the Museum of the Home in Hoxton. Slavery was not a footnote to British history. It helped shape the nation Read more These connections run through the heart of the City of London’s political structure, with several lord mayors commemorated in the Great Hall. Sir William Humphreys, who left legacies to three London hospitals including St Barts, sat on the RAC’s court of assistants from 1683-85 and from 1688-90. In 1711, he attended Board of Trade hearings on the company’s operations on the west African coast, three years before he became lord mayor. His predecessor, Samuel Stanier, who also left money to St Barts in his will, sold off most of his substantial £4,000 holding in the RAC in February 1698, before his lord mayoralty started in 1713. After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans became more formalised and was a lucrative source of funds for merchants. View image in fullscreen Several leading City merchants who invested in companies linked to the enslavement of African people are commemorated in the Great Hall at St Barts. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian View image in fullscreen After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans formalised to become a lucrative source of funds for merchants. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The Great Hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message. Its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – are tied to themes of healthcare. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored last year and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian The private banker Sir Robert Vyner (also known as Viner) became a central figure in the City and was lord mayor of London from 1674-75. He first invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers in January 1663; by August, his holding had grown to two shares, worth £800. In January 1665, he bought a further £1,200 from the Countess of Chesterfield, and was elected to the company’s board where he served from 1667-70. He continued attending board meetings, without formally serving, from 1671 until the company’s dissolution. This positioned him to invest heavily in the RAC, the Adventurers’ successor, subscribing with £5,000 (the equivalent of £1.18m today) and serving as an assistant from 1672-74. During his involvement with both companies, they undertook 81 crossings. Vyner left a portion of the remainder of his estate to St Barts after his death in 1688. Like St Thomas’ hospital in Lambeth, south London, St Barts provided free medical care to the city’s sick and poor people, sustained by charitable donations from City merchants and rental income from land and property across the capital. Last year, the stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. The hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message, its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – all tied to themes of healthcare. St Barts has acknowledged its links to slavery: Barts health NHS trust archives produced an official research guide in 2024 setting out the known history and how to investigate it further, though the trust has not commissioned a stand-alone enslavement report. A spokesperson for the trust said it was “well aware that some notable individuals historically associated with our hospitals profited from the transatlantic slave trade”, and they were identified in the Great Hall because of their donations. “As further information comes to light we are discussing with Barts Charity and Barts Heritage, which manages the listed building, how we could most appropriately acknowledge the full story behind these historic links.” A spokesperson for Barts Charity, which supports the trust, said that, previously, “detailed research has not established whether, or to what extent, particular gifts can be traced into the assets managed by the charity today. We are reviewing the new findings with Barts Health and Barts Heritage and considering any appropriate next steps.” In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a ten-year restorative justice initiative. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters Government struggling to deal with worst crisis in months after being taken by surprise by massive demonstrations By Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Fri 2 Oct 2026 10.10 EDT First published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 08.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A s dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class. “We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.” 1:21 Fires burn as French students protest against lack of investment in education – video “School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers across France : a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during the heatwaves in May and June . View image in fullscreen Students protesting in Lyon on Friday. Photograph: Laurent Cipriani/AP “The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation. She said she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week. Several teachers stood by the barricades in support. The French government is struggling to deal with its worst crisis in months after it was taken by surprise by the thousands of teenagers demonstrating outside schools across the country this week. Students’ unions say the education system is underfunded and neglected. Hundreds of high schools were closed or barricaded on Friday, and hundreds of young people have been arrested as the movement threatens to roll on into next week. Many school students protesting have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education, describing difficult conditions in classrooms with ceilings partially collapsing during class, leaks, cockroaches and buildings in disrepair. Others have spoken of excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff. View image in fullscreen Students kick back teargas canisters in Strasbourg. Photograph: Romeo Boetzle/AFP/Getty Images The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing teargas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday morning, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Léonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east. Several students have been injured in the protests, while the education ministry said 65 education staff were injured, including 40 school principals. An investigation is under way after a 14-year-old boy in Val d’Oise suffered serious injuries to his mouth and jaw after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The family’s lawyer said the boy had thought he was “going to die”. View image in fullscreen Students gather outside the Lycée Voltaire in Paris. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters Outside Lycée Voltaire, riot police stood guard on Friday amid the quiet demonstration by hundreds of children. “We’re totally pacifist,” said Yves, a 17-year-old final year pupil who did not want his name published. He would normally have been in history class but said he had the full support of his parents to be on the barricade. He wanted to study catering next year. “The atmosphere on this barricade is generally very calm,” he said. “But there have been other people from outside school who have come past and tried to set fire to things, so we’ve tried to move the bins to stop that.” View image in fullscreen High-school students face off with riot police in Montpellier. Photograph: Horcajuelo Guillaume/EPA On Friday morning, loud bangs rang out as some people further away from the school let off firework mortars. Yves said: “Yesterday I heard bangs going off every two minutes, it’s loud and scary when things are being fired horizontally and not up into the air. There were people provoking running battles with police but it wasn’t pupils from our school.” Camille, 18, who said he wanted to become a teacher, said pupils were also protesting over the French government’s lack of engagement over poor results in international education rankings. “France has disastrous results and yet we’re one of the countries with the longest school days,” she said. “The government refuses to see that it’s about quality, not the number of teaching hours.” View image in fullscreen Bins burning, with graffiti on one reading ‘fuck RN’, in Paris. Photograph: Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty Images Farther east, on the barricade outside the Lycée Hélène Boucher, students were singing and holding cardboard signs of support for people in Gaza, as well as banners against the far-right presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls. Sofiane, 19, who was studying literature, said students feared the government would scrap its special €1 meals for struggling students and reduce welfare aid for housing. “We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” he said. “It was unbearable sitting exams in 35C-40C heat, even the teachers said those were impossible conditions.” He said the demonstrations were likely to continue. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re doing nothing to remedy that.” Explore more on these topics France Europe Protest news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story G7 to release 100m barrels from reserves to combat surging diesel prices – as it happened France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting Hundreds detained as student protests across France turn violent Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
